name: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony
description: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Thursday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.3rd September: Dr. Rahul KapoorWomen, Work and Well BeingWomen's participation in paid and unpaid work shapes far more than a household budget, it shapes physical, psychological, economic, and social well-being all at once. But that participation is rarely on equal terms: wage gaps, occupational segregation, invisible care work, and the daily balancing act between job and family all take a toll. Dr. Rahul Kapoor, Assistant Professor of Sociology and Social Work at Gautam Buddha University and author of Women and Work: The Sky is Full of Sexism, asks what a genuinely gender-sensitive approach to employment and social protection would actually look like — and why economic participation alone was never going to be enough.17th September: Anukriti AgarwalChacha Knows Best: Chacha Chaudhary and the Politics of NostalgiaBefore Indian households had cable or the internet, they had Chacha Chaudhary — a turbaned uncle whose brain worked faster than a computer, created by Pran Kumar Sharma in 1971. Fifty years on, that same deliberately ordinary uncle now sells toilets, water conservation, and voter turnout on behalf of government ministries. Anukriti Agarwal, a language educator and Fulbright Fellow at Yale, traces how a comic-book uncle went from newsprint to nation-building — and what it reveals when a state borrows the nostalgia the middle class grew up on.24th September: Dr Shashank SinghPrinces in the Polls: Indian Royals and Inherited Power in a Democratic Age, 1948–1967Between the 1950s and 60s, former princely elites didn't disappear from Indian politics — they reinvented themselves within it. Dr Shashank Singh, Junior Fellow at the Prime Ministers Museum and Library and a historian of Gwalior's princely order, uses electoral data and legislative debate from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh to show how monarchical charisma and patronage fused with electoral legitimacy. His argument: India's democratic consolidation didn't dismantle the feudal order so much as absorb and repurpose it.

name: Grounds for Thought: Janpath
description: Grounds for Thought: Janpath, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.17th September: Prateek MundejaWhy Do Good Ideas Fail in Government?Governance is usually discussed in ideals — promises, ambition, the world as it ought to be. Prateek Mundeja, Assistant Professor of Political Science and Mookerjee Fellow (2025–26), argues that the more useful question is a duller one: what actually works? This session takes a realist's tour through limited resources, institutional capacity, and the gap between stated intentions and delivered outcomes — and makes the case that ideals only survive contact with the world when backed by hard, unglamorous choices.22nd September: Aarushee ShuklaThe Pause, The Buzzword, and The CollectiveIn a meeting room in Bihar and Kerala, Aarushee Shukla asked women what their collective meant to them, and got a long, deliberate silence back. That silence, she found, wasn't an absence of an answer — it was its own kind of answer, one we're rarely taught to read. This session recreates that pause live, then turns to the vocabulary — "empowerment," "participation," "social capital" — that runs through women's lives on paper, asking who gets to write those words and who is simply left to live inside them.29th September: Amitrajeet MukherjeeVoices from War: Revisiting John Keegan's The Face of BattleJohn Keegan's landmark book opened with a deceptively simple question — what is it actually like to be in a battle? Fifty years on, his witnesses remain almost entirely European, despite spanning centuries of warfare. Amitrajeet Mukherjee, a doctoral candidate in English Literature at Delhi University, widens that frame to the two and a half million Indians who served in the Second World War — diarists, letter-writers, the censored and the unrecorded — and asks whose voices get to define what "war writing" is for.

name: Heritage Walk of Wazirpur Tomb Complex
description: Delhi's history is often told through its celebrated monuments, yet some of its most fascinating stories survive in places almost forgotten. Hidden behind neighbourhoods, urban landscapes, and everyday life, Wazirpur preserves a remarkable collection of medieval tombs, neglected water structures, and architectural fragments that quietly bear witness to centuries of change. Hidden Heritage of Wazirpur invites participants to step beyond familiar heritage circuits and discover a landscape where silence has become both its greatest mystery and its greatest storyteller.The experience explores monuments that once stood at the heart of thriving settlements but gradually slipped from public memory as the city expanded around them. Through architectural observation, historical context, and field-based interpretation, participants uncover how these overlooked structures reveal stories of patronage, engineering, settlement patterns, and Delhi's evolving urban fabric. Equally, the walk raises important questions about conservation, memory, and the value we assign to heritage beyond UNESCO sites and celebrated monuments. It is an invitation to see the extraordinary in the overlooked and to recognise that every forgotten structure holds the potential to reshape our understanding of Delhi's past.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Delhi's forgotten heritage landscapes and the historical evolution of Wazirpur.Explore the Wazirpur Tomb Complex and understand its architectural significance.Visit hidden medieval tombs scattered across the landscape, discussing their patrons and forgotten histories.Examine surviving historic water systems and their importance in sustaining medieval settlements.Explore lesser-known medieval structures while interpreting architectural features and construction techniques.Discuss urbanisation, neglect and the conservation challenges facing Delhi's undocumented heritage.Encourage participants to observe, document and appreciate overlooked monuments as valuable cultural assets.Closing discussion and photography.

name: unZipping the World: On Absence & Emptiness
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that starts with two letters hiding an entire universe of ideas: U and N.The suffix "Un" — the very one baked into "unLecture" — is a small linguistic trick with outsized power. It hides negation and logic. It has produced social evils like untouchability. And underneath all of that, it's tangled up with some of philosophy's oldest questions about absence and emptiness.This is a joyful reflection on the complexities hiding inside the simplest expressions we use every day — the words so small we never stop to ask what they're actually doing.The session explores:What the prefix "Un" reveals about the hidden logic of everyday languageHow something as small as negation can shape ideas as serious as untouchabilityWhat absence and emptiness actually mean, philosophically speakingA playful, wide-ranging tour through language, logic and lived experienceAbout the SpeakerSundar Sarukkai is a philosopher and writer whose lifelong search for the hidden languages of nature, humans and societies has produced a rich body of work spanning books, articles, plays and novels — including Following a Prayer: A Novel and Water Days: A Novel. His latest book, Homo Philosophicus: Discovering the Spirit of Philosophy in Everyday Life, is an introductory book on philosophy that presents a unified, humanistic approach to the discipline. More of his work can be found at sundarsarukkai.in.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Why Do Good People Commit Crime?
description: About the LectureAre criminals different from us, or does society make them criminals?This lecture starts by exploring how people understand crime across different social, cultural and individual contexts, and challenges the common assumption that crime is committed only by "bad people." Ordinary individuals, it turns out, become involved in criminal or deviant behaviour more often, and more understandably, than we'd like to admit.Through key criminological perspectives, social environment, peer influence, inequality, culture, opportunity, identity and situational factors, alongside real-life examples, case studies and interactive discussion, this session pushes the audience to examine the question at its centre honestly.The session explores:Why the assumption that crime is only committed by "bad people" doesn't hold upThe key criminological perspectives that explain how ordinary people end up committing crimesReal case studies of how social environment, inequality and opportunity shape criminal behaviourWhat genuinely prevents crime, once you understand where it actually comes fromAbout the SpeakerDr. Michael L. Valan is an Associate Professor of Criminology at Jindal Global Law School, O.P. Jindal Global University. He holds a Master's degree and PhD in Criminology from the University of Madras, Tamil Nadu, and has published twenty-three research articles in reputed peer-reviewed journals, including SCOPUS-indexed journals. He received the ISV Fellowship Award in 2016 from the Indian Society of Victimology and is a visiting scholar at the University of Illinois Chicago. He recently secured a research grant from the ICSSR, Government of India, to conduct a major research project on the victims of rescued bonded labourers. His areas of expertise include victimology, policing and crime prevention, and he brings over ten years of research and teaching experience.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Mandi House Heritage Walk:  Cultural Microcosm of India
description: There are places in Delhi that tell the story of power.And then there are places that tell the story of imagination.Join us for a unique heritage walk through Mandi House — Delhi’s extraordinary cultural district and perhaps the closest thing India has to a living artistic republic.This walk explores how, in the decades after Independence, a remarkable vision began taking shape in the heart of the capital: a space where theatre, dance, music, literature, visual arts, cinema, debate, and experimentation could flourish side by side.From the 1950s and 60s onwards, through political support, institutional ambition, and the dreams of generations of artists, Mandi House slowly transformed into a cultural microcosm of India.As we walk through this fascinating neighbourhood, we will uncover the stories behind some of India’s most iconic cultural institutions:From the elegance of Shri Ram Bharatiya Kala Kendra and the legendary Shri Ram Centre for Performing Arts,to the historic Kamani Auditorium and the National School of Drama,from Triveni Kala Sangam and LTG Auditorium,to Sapru House, FICCI Auditorium, the Russian Centre, Modern School, and the beloved Bengali Market.But this is not merely a walk about buildings.It is a walk about ideas.About the making of modern India through culture.About artists, playwrights, dancers, architects, bureaucrats, politicians, and visionaries who together imagined a capital city where art would not remain confined to palaces or elites, but become part of public life itself.We will also trace the older history of the area and uncover an intriguing question:Why is it called *Mandi House*?Who built it?What existed here before this cultural district emerged?And how did this part of Delhi become the beating heart of India’s modern performing arts movement?Expect stories of rehearsals and revolutions, poetry and politics, architecture and activism, cafés and canteens, backstage struggles and artistic triumphs — all woven into the landscape of one of Delhi’s most intellectually alive neighbourhoods.Come experience Mandi House not merely as a location,but as an idea.This walk is being curated & conducted by Darwesh Heritage walks in collaboration with Sabhyata Foundation.

name: 'Doing' Literature: Intimacy, Risk, Pleasure
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that pushes back on everything school taught you about reading. Growing up, we're told that good exam results prove we've gained good knowledge of everything we've read. But we know that the markers of un-success, what we struggle with, what we can't fully express or understand, what we continue to puzzle over, remain the most memorable and meaningful of our engagements with reading.The humanities isn't about drawing a line under a problem with a QED. It isn't a formula that solves the troubles of the world, personal or political. It's about risk, intimacy, pleasure and failure, because it's an encounter with life itself.This lecture thinks through reading and translating literature, particularly poetry: the desire for it, the labour of it, the frustration and thrill of it, the failure and even death of it. Gayatri Spivak called translation "the most intimate act of reading"  a translator's complete surrender to the text. This talk goes further: reading itself is an intimate act, a constant jousting with everything that unsettles us, and translation only deepens it, an erotics that can go very right, or very wrong.The session explores:Why "un-success" is often reading's most meaningful outcomeWhat Gayatri Spivak meant by calling translation "the most intimate act of reading"How risk, intimacy, pleasure and failure define an authentic engagement with literatureWhy the humanities resist the comfort of formulas and easy resolutionsAbout the SpeakerBrinda Bose is Professor at the Centre for English Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University. She taught earlier at Delhi University and was a Fellow of the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library in New Delhi. She has been a Rockefeller Fellow at Bellagio, Italy, at the Humanities Center of Boston University, and at the Camargo Foundation in Cassis, France. Her interests span modernist and avant-garde literature, cinema and other arts, gender and sexualities, and translation. She completed her BA at Presidency College, Calcutta, a second BA and MA at the University of Oxford, and her PhD at Boston University, all in English literature. She was an office-bearer of the Indian Association for Commonwealth Literature and Language Studies (IACLALS) through three terms, twice a jury member for The Hindu Literary Prize, and served on the selection panel for the Rolex Mentor-Protégé Fellowships for Literature in Geneva. She is currently editing two volumes on Indian avant-garde aesthetics and coordinating a project translating from six Indian languages into English.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: Grounds for Thought: Vasant Vihar, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, One Sunday evening. One unsettling conversation.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.20th September: Kavita KrishnanRed Alert: Ukraine, Gaza and the Tearing Down of Universal Human RightsMust Palestinians, Ukrainians, and Uyghurs compete for our solidarity? For anyone who cares about justice, it's become second nature to read the world through a polarised West-versus-Rest lens — pitting solidarity for Gaza against solidarity for Ukraine, or pro-democracy movements in Iran against anti-war and Palestine solidarity movements elsewhere. Kavita Krishnan, Indian activist and author of De-democratisation, pushes back on the premise itself: are the US, China, and Russia really opposing poles, or does Netanyahu's war depend on all three at once? This session asks whether universal human rights can survive Gaza, why Trump's vision of a "multipolar world order" isn't so different from Xi's, Putin's, or Modi's — and how solidarity might be built without polarity.

name: Bulldozers, Bullets, and the Constitution
description: About the LectureFor the last decade or more, the Indian Constitution has played a starring role in the romance of the Indian nation, especially among those who identify as liberals. This lecture sounds a more pessimistic note. It focuses on Article 21, the article that purports to protect life and personal liberty — and asks what its well-documented inadequacies actually mean.A clear view of these gaps should make us question the idea that the Constitution is a solution to our contemporary troubles. In some respects, it may be part of the problem.The session explores:Why Article 21's protections of life and personal liberty are, in practice, woefully inadequateWhat the gap between constitutional promise and constitutional practice revealsWhy treating the Constitution as sacred might get in the way of confronting its limitsHow "colonial law" and the history of civil liberties shaped the Indian constitutional traditionAbout the SpeakerArudra Burra has a background in political philosophy and law. He wandered into Indian constitutional history while working on questions involving the idea of "colonial law" and the history of civil liberties in the Indian constitutional tradition — concerns he is currently exploring in a book project titled Constitutionalism before the Constitution. He is also interested in the connections between Western and Indian philosophical traditions, explored most recently in his paper "What is 'Indian' about Indian Political Thought?" He teaches in the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences at IIT Delhi.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: The Romance of Railway Buildings
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture on the unlikely architects of Indian grandeur:The Indian Railways.During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the Railways built or came to occupy some of the finest public buildings in India, grand stations that still anchor our cities today. This lecture traces the evolution of the architectural styles Railway companies adopted: Classical Revival, Romanesque Revival, Victorian Gothic, Indo-Saracenic, and more, closely following developments taking place in the UK and Europe at the time.Expect deep dives into individual buildings and the architects behind them, and a look at the charm and beauty of colonial railway architecture that most of us walk past without a second glance.The session explores:How Railway companies came to build some of India's finest public architectureThe evolution of styles, from Classical and Romanesque Revival to Victorian Gothic and Indo-SaracenicHow these buildings tracked architectural developments happening in the UK and EuropeStories of individual stations, buildings and the architects who designed themAbout the SpeakerVinoo Mathur joined the Indian Railway Traffic Service in 1971 and served the Railways in various capacities, including as Divisional Railway Manager, Secretary Railway Board, General Manager Northern Railway, and Member Traffic, Railway Board, before retiring in 2008. His career included overseas assignments in Iraq, Mozambique and Jordan. Since retirement, he has served as Managing Director of a Railway joint venture company, an Independent Director on the Board of Indian Oil Corporation, and an Advisor to Japanese consultants for the Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Railway Project. His interest in heritage architecture began while studying history for his Masters, and deepened in 2004 when, as Secretary Railway Board, he was asked to make the case for Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (formerly Bombay V.T.) to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — a case that succeeded. He is currently President of the Rail Enthusiasts' Society.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Ishq & Ibadat is a journey into one such landscape—Nizamuddin, where the boundaries between history, poetry, music, and spirituality dissolve into one another. Along the way, participants explore how Sufism shaped Delhi's cultural imagination through poetry, qawwali, architecture, and everyday traditions that continue to thrive today. More than a chronological account of monuments, the experience invites participants to reflect on a living heritage where faith transcended identity, music became prayer, and words became bridges between people. description: About the LectureWhat do a candy store on Oxford Street, a fake country in Antarctica, and an Italian man pretending to be his own grandmother have in common?No, they're not part of a new Wes Anderson film. name: Rewriting Epics The Feminist Way
description: About the LectureThe Epics have held the Indian imagination since time immemorial, narrated, performed and rendered into cinema again and again. Looking at them afresh means asking the questions they've spent centuries deflecting: the role of women, the contribution of the dispossessed, and the quintessential human questions of survival and existence.A feminist retelling brings the women back to the centre. It strips away the proverbial sheen of the "just" war to focus on the human question underneath. Whether it's the fiery Draupadi, the "manipulative" Satyavati, the warrior queen Chitrangada, Janaki, or the duo of Kaikeyi and Manthara, the Epics allow us to deconstruct these women through a modern feminist lens.The session explores:How feminist retellings of the Mahabharata and Ramayana recentre their women charactersWhat writers like Tagore, Mahasweta Devi, Irawati Karve and Chitra Divakaruni reveal through their retellingsWhy the Epics' "timeless" characters remain contemporary and urgently relevantHow deconstructing canonical narratives changes what the stories are actually aboutAbout the SpeakerDr. Nandini C. Sen is a Professor of English at the University of Delhi — an author, editor, literary critic and storyteller. For nearly three decades, she has explored how literature shapes the way we understand history, identity, gender and the world around us, working across African Literature, Diaspora studies, mythology, postcolonial studies and feminist readings of the Indian epics. Her academic journey has taken her from Delhi to London as a Charles Wallace Scholar, to the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla as a Fellow, and to universities and literary forums across the world. She is the recipient of the Write India Award for creative writing, the Ambassador for Peace Prize for teaching in a slum cluster, and the Best Lecturer's Award from the Government of Delhi. She is the author of the bestselling short story collection The Second Wife and Other Stories, and editor of several acclaimed books.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.
